before: A class describes objects that share the same kinds of data and actions. An object created from the class is an instance. A reading-session instance should hold its own title and minutes. A method is a function defined inside a class that works with an instance. Creating two sessions should create two independent sets of these values.

`class ReadingSession:` starts the class block. The method `__init__` runs when an instance is created, letting you initialize its fields. The double underscores are part of this special method's exact name. Its first parameter, conventionally called self, receives the instance. `self.minutes = minutes` assigns the supplied minutes to that instance's field. The parameter minutes and the field self.minutes are related but different names.

Here is a complete class with independent instances.
```python
class Session:
    def __init__(self, title, minutes):
        self.title = title
        self.minutes = minutes

    def add_minutes(self, amount):
        self.minutes += amount

first = Session("Nature", 15)
second = Session("Art", 25)
first.add_minutes(8)
print(first.minutes)
print(second.minutes)
```
It prints 23 and 25. Session(...) creates an instance and runs its initializer. Calling first.add_minutes(8) supplies first as self automatically and 8 as amount.

The expression `self.minutes += amount` means read the current minutes, add amount, and assign the result back. It is a short form of `self.minutes = self.minutes + amount`. The dot selects an instance field or method. The method changes state; it need not return a number. To inspect the saved duration, read first.minutes after the call.

A second independently runnable example changes both sessions.
```python
class Session:
    def __init__(self, title, minutes):
        self.title = title
        self.minutes = minutes

    def add_minutes(self, amount):
        self.minutes = self.minutes + amount

first = Session("Nature", 15)
second = Session("Art", 25)
first.add_minutes(8)
second.add_minutes(4)
print(first.title, first.minutes)
print(second.title, second.minutes)
```
The lines are `Nature 23` and `Art 29`. Each method call reads and updates only the instance receiving that call.

Put per-session changing data on self. A value assigned directly in the class body is a class attribute and is shared through the class; using a shared mutable list for session data can make sessions interfere. The initializer fields here hold the specific instance's title and minutes. Python uses indentation to separate class, method, and method-body levels, so preserve every level when typing or copying.

Your required class is ReadingSession. Poetry starts at 20 and receives 10 more minutes, reaching 30; History stays at 35. In first.add_minutes(10), self.minutes means the first instance's minutes. The matching math asks for the amount added between 25 and 40: subtract 25 from 40 to get 15. Use addition to update duration and subtraction to find a change between two known totals.
after:
A class describes a kind of object you can make. Each object made from it is called an instance.

Our class describes a reading session. Each session keeps its own title and number of minutes. Making a second session should give it its own values.

`class ReadingSession:` starts the class. Inside it, `__init__` sets up each new session. This setup method is called an initializer. A method is a function defined in a class.

Here, `self` means the session being set up. In `self.minutes = minutes`, the name on the right holds the supplied number. The part on the left saves that number on this session. Keep both underscores before and after `init`.

Watch what happens when only the first session gets more minutes.
```python
class Session:
    def __init__(self, title, minutes):
        self.title = title
        self.minutes = minutes

    def add_minutes(self, amount):
        self.minutes += amount

first = Session("Nature", 15)
second = Session("Art", 25)
first.add_minutes(8)
print(first.minutes)
print(second.minutes)
```
It prints `23`, then `25`. Only the first session changes.

`Session(...)` makes a session and runs its setup. In `first.add_minutes(8)`, Python passes `first` into `self`. The number `8` goes into `amount`.

`self.minutes += amount` reads the saved minutes, adds `amount`, and saves the new total. Here it means the same as `self.minutes = self.minutes + amount`.

The dot selects something that belongs to this session. This method changes its saved minutes, so it does not need to return a number. Read `first.minutes` to see the new total.

Now give each session some extra minutes.
```python
class Session:
    def __init__(self, title, minutes):
        self.title = title
        self.minutes = minutes

    def add_minutes(self, amount):
        self.minutes = self.minutes + amount

first = Session("Nature", 15)
second = Session("Art", 25)
first.add_minutes(8)
second.add_minutes(4)
print(first.title, first.minutes)
print(second.title, second.minutes)
```
It prints `Nature 23`, then `Art 29`. Each call changes only the session before the dot.

Save each session's changing data on `self`. These saved values are called instance attributes, or fields.

A value set directly inside the class, outside its methods, is a class attribute. Objects can share it. If that value is a list, changing the shared list can affect other sessions too.

Keep the indentation: methods sit inside the class, and their instructions sit inside each method.

Build `ReadingSession`. Poetry starts at 20 minutes. Adding 10 makes 30. History starts at 35 and should stay at 35.

In `first.add_minutes(10)`, `self.minutes` is the first session's saved minutes.

For the separate math question, the total grows from 25 to 40. Subtract: `40 - 25 = 15` minutes were added.
